answer: Feature learning in networks faces a trade-off between expressiveness/representational power and tractability (computational cost and optimization difficulty) when choosing the objective: objectives that capture the data's structure richly (such as reconstruction or generative likelihood objectives) can be harder to optimize and slower to train, while simpler objectives are easier to optimize but may learn features less useful for the task. Comparing the two procedures: a supervised procedure (e.g., training with labeled targets and backpropagation on the task loss) typically has lower training-time complexity per task because its objective is directly aligned with prediction and needs no separate pretraining stage, and it usually achieves higher predictive accuracy when sufficient labeled data is available. An unsupervised procedure (e.g., autoencoders, RBMs, or other reconstruction/generative objectives) generally requires more training time, often with a layer-wise or two-stage pipeline, and its learned features are not tailored to a specific label, so its predictive accuracy is often lower on the downstream task, though it can exploit abundant unlabeled data and can serve as a useful initialization or regularizer, sometimes narrowing or reversing the gap when labels are scarce.
